aiAgentFacts.fact: In a 2021 owner-reported survey, 42% of cats with chronic kidney disease (n=43) were observed to defecate less than once per day, compared with 15% of apparently healthy cats (n=124); P<0.0001.
Eighty-five percent of apparently healthy cats in this survey were observed to defecate one or more times per day.
Observed defecation frequency was significantly lower in CKD cats than in apparently healthy cats (P=0.02).
Observed fecal consistency scores were NOT significantly different between CKD and apparently healthy cats — the difference between groups was in frequency only.
Group overlap is substantial: 58% of CKD cats still defecated at least once daily, and 15% of apparently healthy cats did not — the measure separates groups, not individual cats.
The authors concluded that reduced observed bowel movement frequency in CKD cats represents a clinically important variation from normal.
The study compared cats already diagnosed with CKD against a comparison group; it did not follow undiagnosed cats and provides no evidence that litter box tracking detects CKD early.
A secondary aim of the study was to assess owner awareness of bowel movement frequency by comparing predicted with observed counts; the abstract does not report the outcome of that comparison.

historyQuestions: Supported by the study's own method rather than prescribed by it: daily observed defecation count over a defined window, compared against the individual cat's own prior pattern rather than a population rule.
redFlags: Not addressed — this study identifies no red-flag findings and defines no urgency threshold.
differentialDiagnosesMentioned: Not addressed — the study compares CKD cats with apparently healthy cats and does not evaluate other causes of reduced defecation frequency.
recommendedDiagnosticWorkups: Not addressed — no diagnostic workup is evaluated. CKD diagnosis and staging remain clinical and laboratory-based; nothing in this study substitutes for them.

limitations: Small CKD group (n=43) drawn from a self-selected online survey population
Comparison group was 'apparently healthy' by owner report only, without veterinary confirmation — undetected disease in that group cannot be excluded
All data was owner-collected at home with no independent verification of counts or fecal scores
Inclusion required only two or more days of daily observation despite a 7-day protocol, so exposure windows varied substantially between cats
Cross-sectional design on already-diagnosed cats — establishes association, not predictive or screening value
Multi-cat households cannot reliably attribute stools in a shared box to an individual cat, a source of misclassification the design does not resolve
CKD stage was not used to stratify the reported frequency findings in the abstract, so severity-dependence is unknown
